newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador to slow currency depreciation in '98.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador to slow currency depreciation in '98.

text.p: Fidel Jaramillo, head of Ecuador's central bank, said Tuesday he expects the country's currency depreciation rate against the dollar to be reduced to between 16 and 18 percent for next year.
"If things go as we expect, in December we will announce that the rate of depreciation will be lowered to between 16 and 18 percent," Jaramillo said at a forum for foreign investors.
In March, the government of President Fabian Alarcon raised the rate of depreciation to 21 percent from 18.5 percent for this year.

Jaramillo said that a reduction in the rate of depreciation would be compatible with 1998 inflation, forecast at between 20 and 22 percent and that a slower depreciation rate would not represent a revaluation of the sucre currency.
Ecuador has used a crawling peg currency system for the sucre against the dollar since 1994.
Jaramillo added that he was confident this year's projected inflation of between 28 percent and 30 percent will not hinder the government's efforts on the fiscal front.

"(Inflation) is compatible with an expected 1997 fiscal deficit of between 2.5 percent and 2.7 percent" of gross domestic product, said Jaramillo. That is the government's fiscal target for this year.
Although the deficit is currently at 4.6 percent of GDP, economic measures to be announced by Alarcon this week will make it possible to meet the deficit target, the central banker said.
In 1998, the government hopes to reduce the deficit further, to between 1.5 percent and 2.0 percent of GDP, Jaramillo added.
Jaramillo said he saw no threats to exports.
"We do not see risks to traditional exports, although oil exports may fall because of a drop in oil prices," he said.
To offset this situation, the Transecuadorean oil pipeline project to cross the country is being extended, said Jarmillo.
Ecuador ran a trade surplus of $1.402 billion in 1996, with exports totalling $4.89 billion and imports $3.488 billion.
